verdicts.reason: Strongest X point: verifier drawn from a family outside the final panel plus an ambition rating; strongest Y point: simpler PL replacement. X wins on mechanism because it closes Y's own listed failure mode (verifier and panel sharing a family), adds an ambition guard against timid revisions, replays the same opponents for a clean PL refit, and states numeric kill thresholds.

Strongest X point: tau fitted leave-one-brief-out from rating residuals with a min-comparison eligibility guard; strongest Y point: identical core selection rule with fewer moving parts. X wins on evidence because the cluster-correlation strength is estimated from data rather than fixed at 0.5 SD, label consistency is checked (kappa >= 0.6) with a fallback, and kill criteria are numeric.

Strongest X point: witness-value flip requirement that makes rigged always-FAIL checks detectable, plus a claim-count-normalised score; strongest Y point: Min 2023 atomic-claim rationale. X wins on mechanism because unnormalised P-2F in Y rewards cards that emit more claims, and X's 10-brief test with a blinded panel against the single agent plus an ambition guard is the outcome the brief asks for.

Strongest X point: claims are re-extracted from the revised text before the frozen check re-runs, so a developer cannot edit the claim to pass while the card silently changes; strongest Y point: cleaner minimal spec. X wins on fit to the brief because its primary outcome is a blinded held-out-family ranking against the single agent's top 3 across 10 briefs with kill thresholds, whereas Y measures only falsified-claim rate on one brief.

Strongest X point: finals are re-ranked on fresh comparisons so accepted mutants do not carry winner's-curse inflated in-loop scores; strongest Y point: same LUCB-motivated boundary targeting. X wins on mechanism because selection on the same comparisons used to accept variants biases the final ranking upward, and X names a numeric kill (child-beats-parent < 50%) that Y omits.

Strongest X point: fit on panel A and score on panel B of a different family; strongest Y point: same residual-logit design that reduces to BT with few labels. X wins on evidence because Y trains and evaluates on one panel's labels, so leave-one-brief-out AUC would reward learning that panel's biases, which is exactly the Goodhart failure both cards list.

Strongest X point: a 2x2 offline test separating reliability weighting from boundary allocation, plus a 40% per-judge cap; strongest Y point: identical vote model with a clean Fisher-information scheduler. X wins on test design because without the factorial arms a gain cannot be attributed to weighting versus allocation, and the cap prevents the scheduler collapsing onto one judge.

Strongest X point: prior centred on the operator's global win rate and a paired-by-brief primary analysis that respects within-brief correlation; strongest Y point: explicit power calculation. X wins on evidence because Y's per-contest power figure treats correlated contests as independent and so overstates power, while X's hierarchical prior gives sensible behaviour with sparse similar-brief records.

Strongest X point: a same-length no-fix paraphrase placebo through the same gate, so acceptance above placebo measures real repair rather than style drift; strongest Y point: cheaper single-verifier gate with higher expected acceptance. X wins on mechanism because the placebo is the only thing in either card that can distinguish a verifier rewarding rewording from one rewarding fixed weaknesses, and X's primary outcome is the benchmark win vs the single agent.

Strongest X point: tau derived from measured within-cluster correlation and a mean-of-3 non-inferiority cap (reject swaps costing over 1 SE), with output identical to top-3 when finalists are diverse; strongest Y point: same expected-max objective with minimal code. X wins on mechanism because the cap directly neutralises the 'mean-of-3 loses by construction' failure that Y only acknowledges.

Strongest X point: a codebase-probe artifact and a step-0 measurement of checkable-claim fraction with a kill, so the brief's 'implementable in this codebase' rule becomes a decidable check; strongest Y point: ranking under-3-checkable cards last strongly deters hedging. X wins on fit to the brief because assigning pool-median score to sparse-check cards makes qualitative briefs a null rather than a harm, and step 0 tests the core assumption before any build.

Strongest X point: standalone operation with its own extractor fallback, a 1.4x token cap, and an offline test on saved finalists against the single agent's top 3; strongest Y point: fuller 3-iteration loop. X wins on testability because it removes the hard dependency on another card's ledger and measures the brief's actual outcome at bounded cost, whereas Y doubles development tokens and never compares against the single agent.

Strongest X point: gate judges from a family outside both ranker and panel, shown length-normalised fields only, with an explicit overfit-gap metric and kill thresholds; strongest Y point: same targeting logic with less machinery. X wins on mechanism because judge overfitting is the central risk both cards name and only X makes it measurable (gate-family minus held-out rate) and actionable.

Strongest X point: within-run conditional logit cancels brief effects and a staged unlock starts with sign-constrained nuisance weights at about 5 briefs, plus an oracle-headroom kill; strongest Y point: cleaner LC-AlpacaEval analogue that zeroes nuisance terms. X wins on evidence because checking oracle headroom first tells you whether any selection head can gain before fitting one, and the conditional form directly answers the 'brief heterogeneity swamps labels' failure.

Strongest X point: label-free calibration of position, self-preference and shared verbosity terms from probe pairs, with a bias-only arm that needs no external verdicts; strongest Y point: simpler model needing only existing votes. X wins on testability because it cuts the external-label requirement from about 300 to about 100 votes and separates bias correction from reliability weighting, though its authorship-relabelling probe for self-preference is the weakest link.

Strongest X point: offline warm start on saved finalists and a stage-1 chi-square plus leave-one-brief-out log-loss testing whether operators differ at all before any live run; strongest Y point: same bandit design with explicit power numbers. X wins on evidence because it tests the core assumption (operator win rates differ and transfer) cheaply and defines its own contest rule rather than depending on card 0's loop.
